title: Flat Base Breakout
teaches: The flat base breakout as we trade it: a leader rests in a box near its highs above the 50-day and 200-day, the pivot is the base's highest high, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: One, two or three weeks do not get the job done.
facts.claim: IBD: one, two or three weeks do not make a base.

facts.quote: The stock's price declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to intraday trough.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.

facts.quote: The correction within a flat base should be no more than 15% from its intraday high to the bottom of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: the correction inside a flat base is no more than 15%.

facts.quote: It should look like a rectangular box with a correction from high to low of no more than 15%.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base looks like a rectangular box.

facts.quote: the "flat" base has kind of a "U" shape and doesn't look so flat.
facts.claim: IBD allows a flat base with a slight U shape.

facts.quote: Flat bases should show tight trading.
facts.claim: IBD: flat bases should show tight trading.

facts.quote: These shallow patterns often start forming as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base forms as a stock rests after an earlier advance.

facts.quote: In a weekly chart, look for periods of sideways movement or mild declines following a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price.
facts.claim: IBD: look for sideways movement after a prior uptrend of at least 30% (stated for any base).

facts.quote: The typical buy point is the price high made before the decline, plus 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the high before the decline plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: To get the proper buy point, add 10 cents to the highest price in the pattern, which is usually the start of the base.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is 10 cents above the highest price in the pattern, usually the start of the base.

facts.quote: The buy point in a flat base is 10 cents above the left-side high.
facts.claim: IBD: the flat base buy point is 10 cents above the left-side high.

facts.quote: Sometimes you can draw a trend line connecting at least three points along the top of the base and find the lowest potential entry.
facts.claim: IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top of the base.

facts.quote: you want to see volume bulge at least 40%-50% above average when a stock breaks out of the flat base.
facts.claim: IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average.

facts.quote: A breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% in order to be counted as one stage.
facts.claim: IBD: a breakout counts as a stage only if it gained at least 20%.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases often blow up.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base.

facts.quote: One guideline is the 7%-8% sell rule.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is the 7% to 8% sell rule.

facts.quote: Flat bases form over a 5 to 65 week range. The minimum depth is 0% with a maximum of 15%.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base is 5 to 65 weeks long and 0% to 15% deep.

facts.quote: Flat bases often occur after a stock runs up after breaking out of one of the other chart patterns.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: flat bases often follow a run-up out of another pattern.

facts.quote: In the case of a Cup, Flat Base, Consolidation or IPO Base, the Pivot corresponds to the Left Side High that began the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base's pivot is the left-side high that began the base.

facts.quote: In most cases, it is the highest intra-day price over the last 100 days (or 20 weeks)
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the left-side high is usually the highest intraday price of the last 100 days.

facts.quote: The percent decline from the start of the base (left side high) to the bottom (intraday low) of the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith measures depth from the left-side high to the base's intraday low.

facts.quote: Stocks emerging from third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: third, fourth or later stage bases are late and more likely to fail.

facts.quote: The Base Stage and Count are always reset to 1 once an intraday low price undercuts the low of the previous base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the base count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.

facts.quote: The Pivot Range is 0% to 5% above the pivot point
facts.claim: MarketSmith's buy range is 0% to 5% above the pivot.

facts.quote: A prior uptrend of 30% or more: This is the initial strong move that leads into the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a prior uptrend of 30% or more leads into the base.

facts.quote: the stock's price should not fall more than 15% from its highest point within the base.
facts.claim: TraderLion: no more than 15% off the base's high.

facts.quote: the trading volume should be at least 40% higher than its average volume (1.4 times the relative volume).
facts.claim: TraderLion: breakout volume at least 40% above average.

facts.quote: A well-formed flat base should have tight and orderly price action
facts.claim: TraderLion: a well-formed flat base is tight and orderly.

facts.quote: Flat base breakouts are more likely to succeed in a strong, bullish market.
facts.claim: TraderLion: flat base breakouts do better in a strong, bullish market.

facts.quote: In almost all cases, one-, two-, and three-week bases are risky. They should be avoided.
facts.claim: TraderLion, quoting O'Neil: one-, two- and three-week bases are risky.

facts.quote: Wide and loose bases are a big sign of real danger.
facts.claim: TraderLion: wide and loose bases are a sign of danger.

facts.quote: This is nothing but Darvas box setup.
facts.claim: Bonde: the flat base is a Darvas box.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months comes first.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price "surfs" the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day and sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: This method can also be traded by anticipating the breakout but I don't find it as effective
facts.claim: Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective.

facts.quote: If a beginner stick to the 10-day. You wait for the first CLOSE below the 10- day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails on the 10-day and sells on the first close below it.

facts.quote: Price should touch one trendline at least three times and twice on the other trendline, using distinct peaks and valleys
facts.claim: Bulkowski's rectangle touches one line at least three times and the other twice.

facts.quote: Trends downward 70% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: volume inside a rectangle top trends down 70% of the time.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.quote: The pivot is the highest intraday high of the base. IBD adds 10 cents; with market orders the 10 cents does not matter.
facts.claim: The pivot is the base's highest intraday high; IBD's 10 cents does not matter with a market order.

facts.quote: Price trades above the pivot during regular hours. Buy with a market order. Set the alert at the pivot.
facts.claim: The trigger: price trades above the pivot in regular hours; buy at market; alert at the pivot.

facts.quote: The ceiling: two or more separate touches of the top within 0.5 ATR, the first at least 10 sessions back.
facts.claim: The ceiling needs two or more separate touches, the first at least 10 sessions back.

facts.quote: Tight at the end: the last 10 sessions' high-to-low range is at most half the base's depth, or the last 3 sessions include an inside day.
facts.claim: Tight at the end: the last 10 sessions span at most half the depth, or an inside day in the last 3.

facts.quote: On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, and the 50-day is above the 200-day.
facts.claim: On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50 above the 200.

facts.quote: In the base, at least 80% of the closes are at or above the 50-day. A brief shakeout under the 50-day is allowed.
facts.claim: At least 80% of the base's closes hold the 50-day; a brief shakeout is allowed.

facts.quote: A few cents under the breakout day's low.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

facts.quote: The base low is not the stop. It can be up to 15% away (the base's depth) and then breaks A13.
facts.claim: The base low is not the stop; it can be the whole depth away.

facts.quote: After the entry, a close back inside the base under the pivot is a warning, not an exit by itself.
facts.claim: A close back inside the base is a warning, not an exit.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: the base low is undercut. The flat base is off. If price reclaims the low within 3 sessions, it is a U&R setup instead.
facts.claim: An undercut of the base low ends the flat base; a reclaim within 3 sessions is a U&R.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: the base turns wide and loose. The average daily range of the last 10 sessions is larger than that of the base's first 10 sessions.
facts.claim: Wide and loose: the last 10 sessions range wider than the first 10; the base is off.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: a close under the 200-day.
facts.claim: A close under the 200-day before the trigger invalidates the base.

facts.quote: First or second base since the last stage reset. A breakout that gained less than 20% before this base does not count as a new stage; the count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.
facts.claim: First or second base since the last stage reset.

facts.quote: Flat: the least-squares line through the base's closes moves no more than 10% of the base's average close from start to end. A U shape inside that drift is allowed.
facts.claim: Flat: the trend line through the closes drifts no more than 10% of the average close.

facts.quote: The breakout day closes back inside the base, often at its low, and the next session takes the stop.
facts.claim: The failure mode: the breakout day closes back inside the base and the next session takes the stop.

facts.quote: A flat base holds one range about 15% deep or less with a flat top; a VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another, from as deep as 40% down to under 10%.
facts.claim: A flat base holds one range; a VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another.

facts.quote: A flat base falls 15% or less and stays boxy; a cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and then dips again for a handle before the buy.
facts.claim: A cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and dips for a handle; a flat base stays boxy.

facts.quote: A high tight flag nearly doubles (90% or more in 8 weeks or less) and pauses 5 to 30 sessions; a flat base follows a 30% run and rests at least 25 sessions.
facts.claim: A high tight flag nearly doubles and pauses a few weeks; a flat base is a longer rest after a smaller run.

facts.quote: If price broke under it and came back within 3 sessions, the flat base is off and the trade is the reclaim, not the breakout.
facts.claim: After an undercut and a reclaim within 3 sessions the trade is the reclaim, not the breakout.

facts.quote: Putting the stop at the base low (too wide), or pulling it tighter to fit the size.
facts.claim: A named mistake: the stop at the base low, or pulled tighter to fit the size.

facts.quote: Two in three uptrend-rectangle breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days. The day's-low stop will be tested often. That is normal, not a reason to widen it.
facts.claim: Two in three rectangle breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days; the stop is not widened for that.

facts.quote: Volume in the base: the second half of the base averages less volume than the first half. A grade cue, not a gate.
facts.claim: Volume drying up in the second half of the base is a grade cue, not a gate.

facts.quote: Before the trigger: the depth grows past 15%. No longer a flat base; it may become a cup or a double bottom.
facts.claim: Past 15% deep it is no longer a flat base.

facts.quote: fb.breakout_volume: 1.4x the 50-day volume or more, closes near the high
facts.claim: The A+ breakout day: heavy volume and a close near the high.

facts.quote: fb.breakout_volume: light volume, closes mid-range
facts.claim: The B- breakout day: light volume and a close mid-range.

facts.quote: A cue, not a rule: the setup is best when many leaders are basing sideways after a pullback. Bracco steps back when there is a lack of clean, tight bases.
facts.claim: The setup is best when many leaders are basing sideways after a pullback.

facts.quote: The base starts at the left-side high: the highest intraday high of the last 100 sessions.
facts.claim: The base starts at the left-side high, the highest intraday high of the last 100 sessions.

facts.quote: Anticipating inside the base with no trigger.
facts.claim: A named mistake: anticipating inside the base with no trigger.

walkthroughs.title: NUS, September 2013: the textbook shelf
steps: NUS, September 2013. The stock nearly doubled, then shelves six weeks, riding the rising 10 and 21-day. Three taps of 90.
Context and pattern check out: above its 50-day and 200-day, shallow at 10.3%, tight, a flat ceiling. The pivot is 90.
2013-09-09: it trades through 90 on 1.9x volume. Buy at market, 90.01. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 88.22.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base, stop taken next day. Instead it reaches 3R the next session. Trim a third.

walkthroughs.title: ALLY, June 2019: tight at the end
steps: ALLY, 2019. A leader rests 11.2 weeks after a 31% run, only 5.5% deep: the shallowest base of the ten.
Four taps of 30, and inside days into the breakout. That is tight at the end, the rule in one picture.
2019-06-27: it clears 30 on 1.80x volume. Buy at market, 30.28. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 29.79.
Failure mode: a close at the low, back in the base. Instead it grinds to 3R on day 10. Slow still pays.

walkthroughs.title: WSM, September 2023: the throwback and the trims
steps: WSM, 2023. An 8-week shelf, 14.6% deep, four taps, after a 30% run. On 2023-09-25 it breaks out on 4.99x volume.
Buy at market, 73.16. Stop under the day's low, 72.24. 3R the next day: a third off, stop to breakeven.
5R by day 10: another third off. Then a throwback to 71.56, through the pivot and the original stop.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base. It came after both trims were due; the trail rode the run to 99.

questions.q: In one line, what is a flat base?
choices: A boxy rest near highs after a run
A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash
A pole that doubles in a few weeks
A drift under the falling 200-day
questions.answer: A boxy rest near highs after a run
questions.why: A boxy rest near the highs after a run. IBD says a flat base should look like a rectangular box. The correction from high to low is no more than 15%. It forms as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance. It is not a bounce after a drop. It rests near the highs, not under a falling 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is a leader catching its breath in a box near the highs.

wrong.A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash: That is a bottoming pattern after a drop. A flat base rests near the highs after an advance.
wrong.A pole that doubles in a few weeks: That is the high tight flag's pole. A flat base is the rest, not the run.
wrong.A drift under the falling 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. A flat base sits above its rising averages.

questions.simple: A flat base is a strong stock resting in a boxy pause near its highs after a run up.

questions.q: On a flat base, where is the pivot, the level a breakout has to trade through?
choices: The base's highest intraday high
The base's lowest intraday low
The rising 50-day moving average
The midpoint of the base's range
questions.why: The base's highest intraday high. MarketSmith calls it the left-side high that began the base. IBD adds 10 cents to it for the buy point. With a market order the 10 cents does not matter. The lowest low is the floor, and the 50-day is support inside the base.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the box. Mark it before the open.

wrong.The base's lowest intraday low: That is the base low, the floor. The breakout goes through the ceiling.
wrong.The rising 50-day moving average: The 50-day is support inside the base, not the trigger.
wrong.The midpoint of the base's range: Halfway up the box is still inside the box. Nothing has broken out.

questions.simple: The pivot is the top of the box, the highest high of the base, and a breakout must trade through it.

deeper.counter: IBD quotes its buy point 10 cents above the high. We mark the high itself and buy at market as price trades through it. It is the same setup. Only the line you watch sits 10 cents lower.

questions.q: On a flat base breakout the stop goes a few cents under the base low.
questions.why: False. The stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card the breakout day has price above the 50-day and the ___-day, and the 50-day sits above that line.
questions.why: 200. On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, and the 50-day is above the 200-day. The rulebook also bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The 50-over-200 order is our own setup test.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200. Then look at the box.
questions.simple: The blank is 200, because price must sit above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200.

questions.q: A flat base pivot is 60.00. When do you buy?
choices: Trade through 60.00, regular hours
At the first daily close above 60.00
In premarket, if it gaps over 60.00
Inside the base, just under 60.00
questions.why: As it trades through 60.00 in regular hours, bought at market. Set the alert at the pivot and let the trade come to you. Do not wait for the close, and do not buy in premarket. Entries are market orders, and no new buys come outside regular hours. Buying inside the base has no trigger, and Kullamagi finds anticipating less effective.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order, regular hours.

wrong.At the first daily close above 60.00: Our trigger is the trade through the pivot, not the close. Waiting for the close is a different, later entry.
wrong.In premarket, if it gaps over 60.00: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.Inside the base, just under 60.00: That is anticipating with no trigger. Kullamagi finds it less effective; we wait.

questions.simple: Buy with a market order as price trades through 60.00 during regular hours, not at the close or in premarket.

questions.q: Volume drying up in the second half of the base is a grade cue, not a gate.
questions.why: True. Our card treats volume that dries up in the second half of the base as a grade cue, not a gate. A base without it can still trigger. Bulkowski finds that volume inside a rectangle trends down 70% of the time. That says quiet volume is common. It does not say it predicts a better result.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume into the right side is a plus, not a must.
questions.simple: True. Quiet volume in the second half of the base helps the grade, but we do not need it to trade.

questions.q: Our card wants a flat base to be the first or second base since the last stage reset.
questions.why: True. Our card wants the first or second base since the last stage reset. IBD says it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base. MarketSmith says third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail. The count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. The first two are the ones we want.
questions.simple: True. Our card wants the first or second base, because later bases are late in their move and may fail.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Strong sales and earnings count for more than the chart.
questions.why: False. We prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first. Growth helps pick between charts. It does not replace the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help. The chart decides.
questions.simple: False. Strong sales and earnings help, but the chart comes first.

questions.q: Where does a flat base start?
choices: At the left-side high
At the lowest low of the base
At the first 50-day crossover
On the day of the breakout
questions.why: At the left-side high, the highest intraday high of the last 100 sessions. MarketSmith agrees: in most cases it is the highest intraday price over the last 100 days, or 20 weeks. IBD calls it the highest price in the pattern, usually the start of the base. Depth and the pivot both measure from there.
questions.lesson_line: Find the left-side high first. Everything else is measured from it.

wrong.At the lowest low of the base: The low is the bottom of the box, found later. The base starts at its first high.
wrong.At the first 50-day crossover: The 50-day is a line inside the base, not its start.
wrong.On the day of the breakout: That is where the base ends, not where it starts.

questions.simple: A flat base starts at the left-side high, the highest price of the last 100 sessions.

questions.q: Over the last ten sessions a base spans at most half its depth, or the last three include an inside day. Our card's name for it?
choices: Tight at the end
A flat ceiling
A volume dry-up
A held 50-day
questions.why: Tight at the end. Our test: the last 10 sessions span at most half the base's depth, or the last 3 sessions include an inside day. IBD says flat bases should show tight trading.
questions.lesson_line: Tight at the end is the tell. Inside days into the pivot are the picture.

wrong.A flat ceiling: That is the top, touched at least twice. It says nothing about how tight the last ten sessions are.
wrong.A volume dry-up: That is volume fading in the second half of the base, a grade cue. This question is about the price range.
wrong.A held 50-day: That is the closes staying at or above the 50-day. This question is about the range of the last bars.

questions.simple: Tight at the end: the last ten sessions span half the depth or less, or the last three include an inside day.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Does the top count as a flat ceiling?
choices: Yes; the top has been tested enough
Yes, but only after a fourth test
No; there are too few tests here
No; the first test is too recent
questions.answer: Yes; the top has been tested enough
questions.why: Yes. Two or more separate touches of the top make the ceiling. They sit within 0.5 ATR, and the first is at least 10 sessions back. Here there are three, and the first was six weeks ago, well past 10 sessions. Three clean taps is the A+ cue on our card.
questions.lesson_line: A ceiling is touched, not guessed. Two taps make it; three make it clean.

wrong.Yes, but only after a fourth test: Two or more separate touches is the rule. Three already clears it, so no fourth is needed.
wrong.No; there are too few tests here: Two or more separate touches is the rule. Three is more than that.
wrong.No; the first test is too recent: The card needs the first touch at least 10 sessions back. Six weeks ago is well past that.

questions.story: A stock rests nine weeks under 48. It has touched 48 three times, on three swings, all within a few cents, the first six weeks ago. The floor holds near 43.
questions.simple: Yes, because two or more separate touches of the top make a flat ceiling, and this one has three.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's rectangle wants one line touched at least three times and the other at least twice, using distinct peaks and valleys. Our card asks only for two separate touches of the top, the first at least 10 sessions back. Three clean taps just make the top look cleaner.

questions.q: A close under the 200-day before the trigger ends the flat base setup.
questions.why: True. A close under the 200-day before the trigger invalidates the base. The rulebook bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. A brief shakeout under the 50-day is different, and the card allows it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there is no flat base to buy.
questions.simple: True. A close under the 200-day before the buy ends the setup, so there is nothing to buy.

deeper.trap: The two lines are not treated alike. The card allows a brief shakeout under the 50-day. At least 80% of the base's closes must hold it. The card's words for the 200-day are a close under it, and that ends the setup before the trigger.

questions.q: At the breakout the stock is 2% over its pivot and 12% above its 10-day average. Our rule?
choices: Skip it; it is too stretched
Buy; the pivot is what matters
Buy at half the usual size
Buy, but with a tighter stop
questions.answer: Skip it; it is too stretched
questions.why: Skip it. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy. At 12% this one is past the line, even though it is only 2% over the pivot. The pivot is the trigger, but it does not override the stretch rule. Half size and a tighter stop do not change the answer.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout that is already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Buy; the pivot is what matters: The pivot is the trigger, not the whole rule. The stretch rule still applies at the fill.
wrong.Buy at half the usual size: Size does not fix a stretched entry. The rule is skip.
wrong.Buy, but with a tighter stop: A tighter stop does not fix a stretched entry either. The rule is skip.

questions.simple: Skip it, because a stock more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We never buy a flat base breakout more than ___% above the pivot.
questions.why: 4%. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. MarketSmith's buy range runs 0% to 5% above the pivot, so our line is stricter. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The blank is 4, because we never buy more than 4% above the pivot.

deeper.trap: The 5 in the bank is the trap. MarketSmith's range runs to 5% above the pivot, a looser vendor line. Our rulebook cuts it to 4%. Past that, a late buy leaves the stop farther away, so the share count shrinks.

questions.q: A flat base stop that you watch yourself counts as a real stop.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. A level you only watch does not count, even if you plan to act on it.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False. A stop must be a real order with the broker, not a level you only watch in your head.

questions.q: A ten-week base about 10% deep: a level top tapped three times, the same floor each time, one range held. What is this base?
choices: A flat base, still resting
A VCP, with shrinking swings
A cup, with a handle forming
A double bottom, mid-pattern
questions.why: A flat base. At about 10% deep it holds one range with a level top, inside the 15% limit. A VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another, from as deep as 40% down to under 10%. IBD says a flat base should look like a rectangular box. A cup is a rounded fall and recovery with a handle.
questions.lesson_line: One range, one ceiling, the same floor: that is the box. Shrinking swings are the other setup.

wrong.A VCP, with shrinking swings: A VCP tightens pullback by pullback. These swings hold one range.
wrong.A cup, with a handle forming: A cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and then dips for a handle. This base is about 10% deep and boxy.
wrong.A double bottom, mid-pattern: Past 15% deep, a base may turn into a cup or a double bottom. This one is about 10% deep and holds one range.

questions.simple: A flat base, because it holds one range with a level top, while a VCP has swings that shrink.

questions.q: IBD's buy point is the base's high plus 10 cents; our market order at the trade-through makes the 10 cents moot.
questions.why: True. IBD adds 10 cents to the left-side high for its buy point. We mark the high itself and buy at market as price trades through it. So the 10 cents does not matter to us.
questions.lesson_line: Same level, no 10 cents. The pivot is the high; the trigger is the trade through it.
questions.simple: True. IBD adds 10 cents to its buy point, but our market order as price breaks through makes that gap not matter.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: No; wait until it has reported
No; wait one more day, then buy
Yes; the trigger fired this morning
Yes, but at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; wait until it has reported
questions.why: No. We make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. The trigger fired Monday, but the report comes Wednesday after the close, inside that window. A trade already open is held through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout two days before earnings is a coin flip with a story. Wait.

wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Size does not fix a report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.No; wait one more day, then buy: Tuesday is still inside the 3 days before the report. The window runs up to the report.
wrong.Yes; the trigger fired this morning: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no. The earnings rule is a hard line.

questions.story: The base is clean and tight. The pivot is 112.00 and it trades through this Monday morning. Earnings come after the close on Wednesday.
questions.simple: No, because we make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report, and this report is Wednesday.

deeper.trap: The rule is about the date, not the setup. A clean base, a strong trigger or a smaller size do not lift it. It also covers new buys only. A trade already open is held through a report only if it is already up 5R.

questions.q: Where does the first trim come on a flat base winner, by our hard rule?
choices: A third at 3R
Half of it at 2R
All of it at 5R
A third at 1R
questions.why: A third at 3R. That is the hard rule for the first trim. Ideally it can come anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice we mostly wait for 5R. After the first third, another third comes off at 5R. Then the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest.

wrong.All of it at 5R: 5R is the second third, not the exit. The last third rides the trail.
wrong.A third at 1R: 1R is where the time stop looks, not where we sell winners.
wrong.Half of it at 2R: Too early and too much. The first trim waits for 3R.

questions.simple: The first trim is a third of the position at 3R, and the next third comes off at 5R.

questions.q: Bought at 90.01 with the stop at 88.22. One R is the fill minus the stop. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 95.38. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. That is 3R, where the first third comes off. NUS reached it the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap between the fill and the stop, which is 95.38.

questions.q: An RS rating of 85 in one of the weakest groups still meets our leader rule.
questions.why: False. The rule is to buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A rating of 85 in a weak group does not meet it.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base in a laggard is a box going nowhere. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: False. We want leaders with an RS rating of 80 or more in one of the strongest groups.

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. By our guide, which flat bases may you buy?
choices: Only the top grade, A+ setups
Any setup, at the full risk size
None; Orange means all cash
Both A and A+ setups, no others
questions.answer: Only the top grade, A+ setups
questions.why: Only A+ setups. By our guide, Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange is only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the box. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.Any setup, at the full risk size: That is Green. Orange narrows you to A+.
wrong.None; Orange means all cash: Red is mostly cash. Orange still allows the best setups.
wrong.Both A and A+ setups, no others: Orange allows only A+. An A setup waits.

questions.simple: In an Orange market we take only A+ setups, so lesser flat bases wait.

questions.q: What is the trade now?
choices: The reclaim, as a U&R setup
A breakout through the old top
Nothing; the stock is broken
A short, with a stop over 71
questions.answer: The reclaim, as a U&R setup
questions.why: The reclaim, as a U&R setup (an undercut and reclaim). Once the base low is undercut, the flat base is off. If price reclaims the low within 3 sessions, the trade is the reclaim, not the breakout. Here the floor at 71 was undercut Tuesday and reclaimed by Thursday.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the floor and the box is gone. The reclaim is its own trade.

wrong.A breakout through the old top: The undercut ended the flat base. The old pivot is no longer this setup's trigger.
wrong.Nothing; the stock is broken: A quick reclaim is a shakeout, not a break. It is a different setup, not no setup.
wrong.A short, with a stop over 71: It reclaimed within two sessions. Shorting a quick reclaim is fighting strength.

questions.story: A nine-week flat base holds a floor at 71. Tuesday the low prints 70.40, under the floor. By Thursday the stock closes back above 71.
questions.simple: The trade is the reclaim, because the dip under the floor ended the flat base and price came right back.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ is not the stop; it can sit a whole base's depth away.
questions.why: The base low. It is not the stop, and it can be up to 15% away, the base's depth. That breaks our rule that the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the breakout day's low, not the bottom of the box.
questions.simple: The base low is not the stop, because it can sit up to 15% away, far wider than our usual stop.

deeper.trap: Two mistakes are named on the card. One is putting the stop at the base low, which is too wide. The other is pulling the stop tighter just to fit the size. Neither is the fix. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: The lowest low in the two months before the base was 40.00 and the left-side high is 50.00. The prior advance, in percent?
questions.why: 25%. The advance is the gain from the lowest low to the left-side high, divided by the low: 50 minus 40, over 40. IBD looks for a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price. Kullamagi looks for a move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months. A 25% run is under both lines.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A box with no run in front of it is just a box.
questions.simple: The run is the gain from the low to the high, divided by the low, which is 25% here.

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00, the base's lowest intraday low 86.50. How deep is the base, in percent?
questions.why: 13.5%. Depth is the left-side high minus the base's lowest intraday low, divided by the high: 100 minus 86.5, over 100. MarketSmith measures it that way. IBD says a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.
questions.simple: Depth is the drop from the high to the low as a share of the high, which is 13.5% here.

questions.q: Fill 72.20. The breakout day's low is 70.75 and the stop sits five cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.08%. The stop sits five cents under the breakout day's low, so 70.70. Measured against the 72.20 fill, that gap is 2.08%. It is inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. The day's low here is made up for the drill.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop sits 2.08% below the fill, inside the 3% it usually stays within.

deeper.example: APH, trigger 2026-01-12: bought at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70, 2.1% away. The trade ran to 7.6R and reached 3R on day 3. The stop was set from the day's low first, and the size followed from it.

questions.q: Bought at 30.28, stop 29.79. The stock trades to 32.73. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop, and the gain is counted in those units. At 32.73 the stock is five R above the 30.28 fill. That is where the second third comes off, after the first third at 3R. ALLY took ten days just to reach 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.
questions.simple: The gain is five times the fill-to-stop gap, so it is 5R and the second trim comes off.
