questions.q: What now?
choices: Hold; the stop is still the exit
Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed
Widen the stop under the base low
Add to it; the price is lower
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A close back inside the base is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. Here the day closed at 178.15, above the 178.10 stop. In the real AMZN case the next session's low took the stop, a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision, and it was made before the open.

wrong.Widen the stop under the base low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed: A weak close is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Add to it; the price is lower: A weak close is a warning, not a reason to put more money in.

questions.story: You bought the breakout with the stop at 178.10. The day closes at 178.15, its low, back inside the base, just above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold, because a weak close back inside the base is only a warning and the stop is still the exit.

deeper.example: This is AMZN. The breakout day closed at 178.15, the low of its range, back inside the base, on 0.72x volume. The next session's low of 176.75 took the 178.10 stop. The weak close was the warning. The stop did the exit, as planned.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
Buy at market, stop at the base low
Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit
Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
questions.why: Buy. 91.80 is inside our chase line: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. The stop stays a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is too wide, and pulling the stop in to fit the size is also a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Late is not too late. Inside the chase line, buy, and keep the stop under the day's low.

wrong.Buy at market, stop at the base low: The base low is not the stop. It can sit a whole base's depth away. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
wrong.Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit: Pulling the stop tighter to fit the size is a named mistake. The stop comes first and the size comes from it.
wrong.Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase: The chase line is more than 4% above the buy point, not any price past it. 91.80 is inside the line.

questions.story: The pivot is 90.00. You missed the open. At 10:15 the stock trades 91.80.
questions.simple: Buy at market with the stop under the day's low, because 91.80 is inside the chase line.

deeper.trap: Passing feels safe, but the rule is a line, not a ban on late buys. Past 4% you skip it. Inside it you buy, and the stop stays under the day's low. Chasing costs size: the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

questions.q: By the gap rule, where is the stop now?
choices: 50.30, the first 30-minute low
50.95, the first 30-minute high
Sell it all at the open, 50.60
Get out, the gap is past 2R
questions.why: 50.30, the first 30-minute low. A gap through the stop hands the decision to the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day. The low of that first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. The loss down to 50.30 is under 2R, so the 30-minute low stands.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Get out, the gap is past 2R: The 30-minute low is inside 2R here. The ceiling has not been hit.
wrong.Sell it all at the open, 50.60: The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes the decision. The open is not the decision; the 30-minute low is.
wrong.50.95, the first 30-minute high: The new stop is the low of that first bar, not the high.

questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with the stop at 51.00. It gaps open at 50.60, under your stop, so the gap rule applies. The first 30 minutes trade between 50.30 and 50.95.
questions.simple: The new stop is 50.30, the low of the first 30 minutes, because that loss is still inside the 2R limit.

deeper.trap: A stop normally only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception. That is why the new stop, 50.30, sits below the old one at 51.00. The open at 50.60 is not the decision either.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Set the alert at the ___ and buy as price trades through it in regular hours.
questions.why: The pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order as it trades through, regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: Alert at the pivot. Then the market comes to you.

questions.q: A tight base has a 44.00 pivot and sits at 43.20 on an inside day. Buying it now, before the trade-through, is a named mistake on our card.
questions.why: True. The trigger is the trade through the pivot in regular hours, here 44.00. Anticipating inside the base with no trigger is a named mistake on our card. Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective. An inside day shows the base is tight. It is not the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Feeling it coming is not a trigger. The pivot is.
questions.simple: Buying before the trade-through is anticipating, and the buy is the move through 44.00.

questions.q: On a normal day with no gap, a flat base trade that trades down to its stop is sold at the stop.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule, which does not apply on a normal day. When price trades down to it, the exit is taken.
questions.lesson_line: My stop is my stop. That is the whole rule.
questions.simple: True. The stop is the exit, so on a normal day you sell when price reaches it and do not move it wider.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Hold; the stop stays where it is
Widen the stop to give it room
Sell it; the breakout has failed
Raise the stop up to the pivot
questions.answer: Hold; the stop stays where it is
questions.why: Hold it. The stop only moves up, never down or wider, and nothing here calls for raising it. A pullback to the pivot is normal. Our card notes that two in three rectangle breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days.
questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: Never wider. The rule has one exception and this is not it.
wrong.Sell it; the breakout has failed: A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. The stop decides, not the retest.
wrong.Raise the stop up to the pivot: The stop only moves up, but nothing here calls for it. A stop at the pivot sits on the price and invites a stop-out on noise.

questions.story: Three days after the breakout at 73.16, price slides back to the pivot, 73.00. Your stop is 72.24.
questions.simple: Hold with the stop where it is, because a pullback to the pivot is normal and a stop is never widened.

deeper.example: WSM reached 5R by day 10, so both trims were due. In late October it threw back to 71.56, through the pivot and the original stop. That is the two-in-three throwback in person. The stop is not widened for it, and a new buy needs a new trigger and its own stop.

questions.q: By our rule, when does the stop ideally move to breakeven on a flat base winner?
choices: Between 2R and 5R
Between 0.5R and 1R
Between 1R and 1.5R
Between 6R and 8R
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, ideally. That is our guide for the breakeven move. The stop only moves up, so moving it to breakeven is allowed. The hard rule in this part of the plan is the first trim, a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, ideally. The first trim, a third at 3R, is the hard rule.

wrong.Between 0.5R and 1R: Earlier than our guide. It puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
wrong.Between 6R and 8R: Later than our guide. It puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
wrong.Between 1R and 1.5R: Earlier than our guide. It puts breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.

questions.simple: Move the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, ideally.

questions.q: A flat base trade sits at 0.6R after 12 trading days. We keep holding it and let the stop decide.
questions.why: False. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. We do not hold it until the stop is hit.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: False. If a trade is still under 1R after 10 trading days, we sell it and free the money.

questions.q: What do you do on Friday?
choices: Sell a third, right at the open
Wait and decide at the close
Sell the whole position now
Hold it all; the stop is enough
questions.answer: Sell a third, right at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. The open here is 3.4R, past the 3R level, so the first third comes off at once. The rest waits for the 5R trim and then the trail.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait and decide at the close: The level is already passed. Waiting gives the gap a chance to fill.
wrong.Sell the whole position now: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Hold it all; the stop is enough: The stop stays, but the trim is the rule when a level is passed at the open.

questions.story: Your flat base long sits at 2.6R at Thursday's close. Friday it gaps open to 3.4R.
questions.simple: Take the first third at the open, because the stock opened past the 3R trim level.

deeper.example: Gaps happen. Friday's open is already past 3R, so the level is behind you before you can act on it. Waiting for the close only gives the move a chance to fade. The rule takes the trim at the open and leaves the rest to 5R and the trail.

questions.q: Which is the one thing you never do?
choices: Pull the stop in to fit your size
Skip it when the stop will not fit
Move the stop up as the trade works
Set the stop first, then find the size
questions.answer: Pull the stop in to fit your size
questions.why: Never pull the stop in to fit the size. The stop comes first, and the size comes from the stop. By default it sits a few cents under the day's low. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Putting the stop at the base low is the opposite mistake, because that is too wide.
questions.lesson_line: Never pick a size first and back-fit the stop. The stop comes first.

wrong.Skip it when the stop will not fit: Skipping is allowed. The rule says to skip when the honest stop does not fit the risk.
wrong.Set the stop first, then find the size: That is the rule itself. The stop comes first and the size comes from it. The thing you never do is bend the stop to fit the size.
wrong.Move the stop up as the trade works: That is allowed. The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.story: The breakout fills at 48.60. The day's low sits at 46.40.
questions.simple: We never squeeze the stop in just to fit our size, because the stop comes first and the size comes from it.

deeper.trap: The trap is sizing first. You pick the position you want, then choose the tight stop that makes the math work. The stop no longer sits where the chart puts it. The honest stop comes first, and if it does not fit the risk, you skip the trade.

reasons: owner rulebook A3/A4 (stop first, stop never moves wider)
held decision D-005 (what to do when the honest stop is wider than usual) is not keyed: the choices carry no stop percent

questions.q: A flat base is the stock's fourth since the last stage reset. The shape is clean. What does the stage tell you?
choices: Late in the move; likelier to fail
A proven trend; the base is safer
Nothing; the stage does not matter
Early in the move; room to run
questions.answer: Late in the move; likelier to fail
questions.why: Late in the move, and likelier to fail. IBD says breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up. MarketSmith says stocks from third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail. Our card wants the first or second base since the last stage reset. A clean shape does not change the count.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box on the fourth floor is still the fourth floor.

wrong.A proven trend; the base is safer: A long trend means the move is late, not proven. IBD says breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
wrong.Nothing; the stage does not matter: Stage matters. Our card wants the first or second base, and MarketSmith calls later bases more likely to fail.
wrong.Early in the move; room to run: Backwards. A fourth base comes after three earlier ones, so the move is late, not early.

questions.simple: A fourth base is late in the move, and a clean shape does not change that.

deeper.trap: The trap is a beautiful box. A fourth base can look like a perfect rectangle with tight closes and still sit late in the move. Shape and stage are separate rows. The count only goes back to 1 once an intraday low undercuts the low of the previous base.

reasons: card base-count line is proposed and the owner may want a third base graded B- instead of a pass
MarketSmith wording is hedged (may be more likely)

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job: a small planned loss
Cost you the trade; it needed room
Protected you from losing anything
Proof the setup was bad; drop it
questions.answer: Its job: a small planned loss
questions.why: Its job: a small, planned loss. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. You bought at 241.28 and the stop at 236.86 was hit on day 1, with a low of 232.68. Two sessions later it closed at 216.08, 10% under the fill. Giving it room would have been a 14% hole in three sessions. A stop hit still books a loss, and one stop-out does not judge the setup. That loss is the cost of being there for the ones that work.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Cost you the trade; it needed room: Room was a 14% hole in three sessions. The stop saved most of it.
wrong.Protected you from losing anything: A stop hit still books a loss. You bought at 241.28 and the stop sat at 236.86. The stop keeps the loss small.
wrong.Proof the setup was bad; drop it: One stop-out does not judge a setup. A loss taken at the stop is the system working, and the next trigger is a new trade.

questions.story: You bought the gap open at 241.28, above the pivot. It closes mid-range on average volume. Next day the low hits your stop at 236.86. Two sessions later it closes 10% under your fill.
questions.simple: The stop did its job. It cut a small planned loss before the stock fell much further.

deeper.example: META, 2020-06-23: bought at 241.28 with the stop at 236.86, 1.83% under the fill. The stop was hit on day 1, and the trade never showed a gain (best 0.0R). The loss was small and planned. Holding on would have meant a 14% hole in three sessions.

reasons: owner rulebook A4 (the stop is the exit)

questions.q: On our card, which breakout day is the stronger one?
choices: The 1.9x day closing at the high
The 0.8x day; quiet is better
Equal; only the pivot matters
Neither; skip any day under 2x volume
questions.answer: The 1.9x day closing at the high
questions.why: The 1.9x day closing at the high. Our card's A+ breakout day is 1.4x the 50-day volume or more with a close near the high. The B- day is light volume and a mid-range close. IBD also wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average. The card needs the volume for an A or A+ grade, not to take the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a strong close make the stronger day. Light volume and a mid-range close make the weaker one.

wrong.The 0.8x day; quiet is better: Quiet is for inside the base. The breakout wants a crowd.
wrong.Equal; only the pivot matters: The pivot is the trigger. The day's volume and close are the cue.
wrong.Neither; skip any day under 2x volume: There is no 2x bar. IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average, and the 1.9x day has it.

questions.story: Same base, two breakout days. One trades through on 0.8x its 50-day average volume and closes mid-range. The other on 1.9x and closes at the day's high.
questions.simple: The day with heavy volume and a close at the high is the stronger one.

reasons: held decision D-006 (is breakout volume a grade cue or a gate) is on a provisional default

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: Wide and loose; the base is off
Still a flat base; the top holds
It will tighten; the base stays on
Fine; only the depth matters here
questions.answer: Wide and loose; the base is off
questions.why: Wide and loose, so the base is off. Our test: the average daily range of the last 10 sessions is larger than that of the base's first 10 sessions. The story has exactly that, so a flat top does not save it. A box that gets louder as it goes is unwinding, not resting.
questions.lesson_line: A box that gets louder as it goes is not resting. It is unwinding.

wrong.Still a flat base; the top holds: A flat top over widening bars is a ragged box. The ranges are the tell.
wrong.It will tighten; the base stays on: Hope is not a setup. The test is the ranges now, and the last 10 sessions are wider than the first 10.
wrong.Fine; only the depth matters here: Depth is one test. Our card also checks the ranges, and the last 10 sessions are wider than the first 10.

questions.story: Six weeks into a base, the daily bars have grown. The last ten sessions swing wider every day than the first ten did. The top is still flat.
questions.simple: The daily swings keep growing, so this is not a calm rest and we call the base off.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the owner reviews it)

questions.q: Does the base still hold the 50-day by our card?
choices: Yes; a brief shakeout is allowed
No; one close under kills it
No; it must never touch the 50-day
Yes; only the breakout day checks it
questions.answer: Yes; a brief shakeout is allowed
questions.why: Yes. Our card wants at least 80% of the base's closes at or above the 50-day. A brief shakeout under it is allowed. Two closes under in an eight-week base is well inside that line. Kullamagi says price sometimes toes the 50-day while it rests. What would fail is a stock that lives under the 50-day, not one that touches it.
questions.lesson_line: Holds the 50-day means most closes, not every close.

wrong.No; one close under kills it: Two closes under in an eight-week base is well inside the 80% line.
wrong.No; it must never touch the 50-day: Touching the 50-day is normal in a rest. Living under it is the problem.
wrong.Yes; only the breakout day checks it: Wrong reason. The card also checks the base itself: at least 80% of the closes at or above the 50-day. That is why a brief shakeout still passes.

questions.story: In an eight-week base the stock closed under its 50-day on two days, a quick dip. Then it sat back above it for the rest.
questions.simple: Yes, because most closes held the 50-day, and a quick dip under it is allowed.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the owner reviews it)

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 59.40, stop 57.96. No position cap applies. How many shares?
questions.why: 173 shares. The dollar risk is the account times the risk percent, which is 0.5% of 50,000. The risk per share is the fill minus the stop, 59.40 minus 57.96. Divide the first by the second and round down. The size is the smaller of that and the position cap, and no cap binds here. The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Divide the dollar risk by the distance and round down.
questions.simple: Divide the dollar risk by the gap between fill and stop, then round down to 173 shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is rounding up. Rounding a share count up risks slightly more than the 0.5% you chose, and the formula rounds down for that reason. Dividing the dollar risk by the entry price instead of the entry minus the stop is the other common slip.

questions.q: The last third of a flat base winner trails the 10-day or the 21-day. It is sold on the first touch of the line.
questions.why: False. We sell the last third on a close below the line, not on a touch. The line is the 10-day average for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one. Kullamagi's beginner rule also waits for the first close below the 10-day. An intraday dip under the line is not an exit.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.
questions.simple: False, because we sell on a close below the line, not when price merely touches it.

reasons: owner rulebook E52 (trail and close-below rule)

questions.q: Take the breakout?
choices: No; it fails both of our floors
No; only the price floor fails
Yes; the base is clean enough
Yes, but at half our normal size
questions.answer: No; it fails both of our floors
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This stock fails both: it costs $7 and trades about $4 million a day. The rule comes before the chart, so a clean base does not rescue it. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: A clean box in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; the base is clean enough: The base is fine and the stock is not ours. The liquidity rule comes before the chart.
wrong.Yes, but at half our normal size: Size does not make a thin stock liquid.
wrong.No; only the price floor fails: The $4 million a day misses the $20 million floor too. Both floors fail.

questions.story: A clean flat base on a $7 stock that trades about $4 million a day.
questions.simple: No, because the stock costs too little and trades too little, and a clean chart does not change that.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (B23)

questions.q: The stock trades 2,000,000 shares a day on average. Our ceiling on the position?
choices: 20,000 shares
40,000 shares
200,000 shares
No cap if the stop is tight
questions.why: 20,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 2,000,000 is 20,000. A tight stop does not lift the cap. Illiquid stocks are not even watched. The risk-based size has to fit under this ceiling too.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.200,000 shares: That is ten times our line. The ceiling is 1% of the daily volume.
wrong.40,000 shares: That is double our line. The ceiling is 1% of the daily volume.
wrong.No cap if the stop is tight: A tight stop does not lift the cap. We never own more than 1% of the average daily volume.

questions.simple: We never own more than one percent of the average daily volume, so two million a day means at most 20,000 shares.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (D42)

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A cup with handle
A flat base
A high tight flag
A double bottom
questions.why: A cup with handle. A flat base stays boxy and falls 15% or less. This one fell 24% in a rounded U, climbed back near the high, then dipped just under it. That last dip is the handle. IBD and MarketSmith both cap the flat base at 15% deep. It is not a high tight flag, because that needs a pole that nearly doubles and this run was 60%. Our card has a cup falling 12% to 33%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth. Past the box, it is a cup, with its own rules.

wrong.A flat base: 24% is past every flat base line. The U shape says cup as well.
wrong.A high tight flag: A flag needs a pole that nearly doubles and a short pause. This is a long rounded fall.
wrong.A double bottom: The story is one rounded fall and a climb back, not two separate lows.

questions.story: The stock ran 60% into a high, then fell 24% over ten weeks in a rounded U. It climbed back near the high. Now it dips a few percent just under the high.
questions.simple: It is a cup with handle, because a flat base never falls past 15% and this one fell 24%.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging by the look. A rounded base near the high can feel flat. Measure it. IBD and MarketSmith stop a flat base at 15%, and this one is 24% deep. The small dip at the end is not a flat base tightening. It is the handle before the buy.

reasons: held decision D-043 (flat base depth) is not keyed: 24% is past every option
the card's cup range of 12% to 33% is narrower than MarketSmith's, so only the 24% is keyed

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A high tight flag
A flat base
A cup with handle
A VCP, shrinking pullbacks
questions.why: A high tight flag. The stock doubled in six weeks, which is the pole. Then it paused in a tight range near the top. Our card says a high tight flag nearly doubles first, then pauses a few weeks. A flat base is a longer rest after a smaller run. The 8% depth does not name it. The run does.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is a flag. Ran and rested for weeks is a box.

wrong.A flat base: The doubling pole names the setup. A flat base follows a smaller run and rests longer.
wrong.A cup with handle: No rounded fall here. A tight shelf on top of a pole is the flag.
wrong.A VCP, shrinking pullbacks: A VCP needs pullbacks that shrink one after another. This is one tight pause on top of a pole.

questions.story: The stock doubled in six weeks on news, then paused twelve sessions in a tight range near the top. The pause is 8% deep.
questions.simple: A pole that nearly doubles and a short pause on top is a high tight flag, not a flat base.

deeper.trap: The pause is only 8% deep, which looks like a flat base. Depth does not separate the two setups. The run does. A flat base follows a smaller run, around 30%, and a flag follows a pole that nearly doubles. Writers differ a little on the exact pole size, but a stock that doubled in six weeks clears every version.

reasons: held decision D-042 (flat base minimum length) is not keyed
the card's flag pole size is stricter than some public write-ups, so the pole is not keyed on a number

questions.q: Is it a flat base?
choices: No; it is too deep for a flat base
No; it is really a high tight flag
Yes; three taps are what count
Yes; IBD allows flat bases to 20%
questions.answer: No; it is too deep for a flat base
questions.why: No. This base is 18.5% deep, and past 15% it is no longer a flat base. IBD's limit is 15% from the intraday peak to the intraday trough, and MarketSmith's is 15% too. Depth runs from the left-side high to the base's intraday low. Three taps do not fix depth, and the 51% run before it is only context. Our scan read it as cup-shaped: best 1.1R, then stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Three taps do not fix a deep base. Depth is a gate.

wrong.No; it is really a high tight flag: A high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more. This run was 51%.
wrong.Yes; three taps are what count: The ceiling is one gate; depth is another. This fails depth.
wrong.Yes; IBD allows flat bases to 20%: IBD's limit is 15% from the intraday peak to the intraday trough. MarketSmith agrees. 18.5% is past that.

questions.story: A 27-session rest after a 51% run, three taps of the top, but the low sits 18.5% under the left-side high.
questions.simple: No, because a flat base can be at most 15% deep, and this one is 18.5% deep.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting taps first. Three clean taps of the top feel like a flat base, so you stop measuring. Measure depth first, from the left-side high down to the intraday low. This one is 18.5% deep by our scan, past the 15% line. After a 51% run it looks like a rest, but the pattern still has to be shallow.

reasons: held decision D-043 (flat base depth) is not keyed: 18.5% is past every option
the 18.5% is our scan's own number

questions.q: Take it as a flat base?
choices: No; the 50-day is under the 200-day
Yes; price is above both
Yes; the 50 is close enough
questions.why: No. Our card wants the close above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200. A base built in a recovery out of a downtrend is not a leader resting. It worked, and it is still not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Price above both lines is half the check. The 50 over the 200 is the other half.

wrong.Yes; price is above both: Price above both with the 50 under the 200 is a recovery, not a leader's rest.
wrong.Yes; the 50 is close enough: Close enough is under. The order of the lines is the rule.

questions.story: A 28-session base after a 42% rebound out of a downtrend. On the breakout day the close is 14% above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits 1.6% under the 200-day.

questions.q: The trend line through the closes rises 4% of their average from start to end. That still counts as flat on our card.
questions.why: True. Flat means the line through the base's closes moves no more than 10% of the base's average close from start to end. A 4% drift is inside that. A slight U shape inside that drift is allowed too. IBD says a flat base can have a U shape and not look so flat. The test uses the closes, not the lows.
questions.lesson_line: Flat is a ceiling and a small drift, not a ruler.
questions.simple: True, because a drift of 4% is well inside the 10% that our card allows.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading flat as level. The test is a trend line through the closes, so a slight slope or a shallow U passes. Judge the drift against the average close, not by eye.

reasons: card criterion is proposed (the 10% drift is a card number)

questions.q: What was the lesson?
choices: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
Never buy on heavy volume
Widen the next stop to the base low
Skip breakouts that gap down
questions.answer: A stop inside the noise gets shaken out
questions.why: A stop inside the stock's normal daily range gets shaken out by noise. You never pull a stop in to fit; and the re-entry on the reclaim is a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop that sits inside a normal day is not a stop. It is a coin flip.

wrong.Never buy on heavy volume: Volume was not the problem. The stop's distance was.
wrong.Widen the next stop to the base low: The base low is too far the other way. The honest stop is the day's low, judged against the range.
wrong.Skip breakouts that gap down: The gap came after the buy. The lesson is about where the stop sat.

questions.story: Breakout on heavy volume, but it closes near the day's low. Your stop sits 0.88% under the fill while the stock's average daily range is 2.5%. Next morning a 2% gap down takes the stop; then it reclaims the pivot and runs.

questions.q: Bought at 73.16, stop 72.24. Where is 5R?
questions.why: 77.76. One R is the fill minus the stop; five of those above the fill. WSM got there by day 10, then threw back through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Know 5R before the open too. The second third comes off there.

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
choices: Sold; it closed under the trail line
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Sold only if it closes under the base
Held; a trail line is only a guide
questions.answer: Sold; it closed under the trail line
questions.why: Sold. The last third trails the 10-day for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one. The exit is a close below the line, and this stock just made one. Breakeven is the floor, not the exit. You trimmed a third at 3R and a third at 5R, so only the last third is left. APH later failed back through the base, to a low of 63.10. The trims and the trail kept it a win.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, the last third on the trail. The close below the line is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for the last third.
wrong.Sold only if it closes under the base: That gives back most of the move. The trail line is closer.
wrong.Held; a trail line is only a guide: The trail line is the exit rule for the last third. A close below it means sell, not wait.

questions.story: You bought at 72.20, stop 70.70. It hits 3R on day three and 5R by day ten; you trimmed a third at each. Then it rolls over and closes below its trail line.
questions.simple: The last third is sold, since a close below the trail line is the exit.

deeper.example: APH, 2026-01-12: bought at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70. It reached 3R on day 3 and 5R by day 10, then failed back through the base with a low of 63.10. Two thirds were banked and the trail took the rest, so it stayed a win: 7.6R in our scan.

reasons: owner rulebook E52 (which trail line fits which stock)
the story does not say whether the stock is fast or steady; both lines break on a close below

questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No; a planned loss on a weak day
Yes; you should have sold at 1.63R
No, but widen the stop next time
Yes; light volume meant skip it
questions.answer: No; a planned loss on a weak day
questions.why: No. A loss taken at the stop is the system working. The stop is the exit, a few cents under the day's low. By our current default, light volume lowers the grade. It does not cancel the trade. You bought at 206.85 with the stop at 203.95. Volume ended at 0.5x. It reached 1.63R, then the stop was hit on day 6 with a low of 203.46.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume lowers the grade, not the rule. A loss at the stop is the plan working.

wrong.Yes; you should have sold at 1.63R: The first trim is a third at 3R. Selling at 1.63R is fear, not a rule.
wrong.Yes; light volume meant skip it: By our current default, volume is a grade cue, not a gate. Light volume lowers the grade; it does not cancel the trade.
wrong.No, but widen the stop next time: The stop only moves up, never wider. A few cents under the day's low is the rule.

questions.story: A clean six-week shelf, four taps, volume drying up. You buy at market at 206.85 as price trades through the pivot, stop 203.95. By the close, volume is only 0.5x and it sits low in its range. It reaches 1.63R, then the stop is hit on day six.
questions.simple: No, the loss was planned. The stop took us out, and light volume only lowers the grade of the day.

deeper.trap: The trap is hindsight. The trade lost, so the weak volume looks like the cause. But volume is a grade cue, not a gate, so the card still allowed the trade. Judge the process: the entry, the stop and the size followed the rules. The peak of 1.63R is no reason to have sold early, since the first trim is a third at 3R.

reasons: held decision D-006 (volume as a gate or a cue) is on a provisional default

questions.q: On our default plan, what came off on the way up?
choices: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
Nothing; it only trails the stop
All of it at 5R, in one sale
Half at 2R and the rest at 5R
questions.answer: A third at 3R and a third at 5R
questions.why: A third at 3R and a third at 5R. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R. Another third comes off at 5R, and the last third trails. That banks two thirds. Move the stop to breakeven, ideally between 2R and 5R. BAC reached 5R in about three weeks, then fell back into the base with a low of 22.16. The trims are what made it a win.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are what you keep when the box pulls it back.

wrong.Nothing; it only trails the stop: Selling nothing lets a 5R trade fall back. BAC fell back into the base after 5R.
wrong.All of it at 5R, in one sale: The last third rides the trail. 5R is the second trim, not the exit.
wrong.Half at 2R and the rest at 5R: The first trim is a third at 3R, not half at 2R. Another third comes off at 5R, and the last third rides the trail.

questions.story: Five taps of a 23.5 ceiling after a vertical run. You bought at 23.56, stop 23.12. It reaches 5R in about three weeks, then sinks back into the base.
questions.simple: We sell a third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

deeper.example: BAC, 2017-02-14: bought at 23.56 with the stop at 23.12 after five taps of the ceiling. It hit 5R in about three weeks, then fell back into the base. The case for the trims: two thirds were already banked at 3R and 5R, and the rest rode the trail.

reasons: B19 also says in practice he mostly waits for 5R; the hard rule is keyed

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Yes; a new trade with a new stop
No; one try per base is the limit
Yes, with a wider stop this time
No; wait for a fresh base to form
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade with a new stop
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Here the stock traded back through the pivot, so it triggered again. The new stop is a few cents under the new day's low, not wider. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: The stop is the day's low again. A wider stop to avoid a repeat is the mistake.
wrong.No; one try per base is the limit: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.No; wait for a fresh base to form: The base is still there and it triggered again. That is the re-entry.

questions.story: Stopped out of a flat base breakout on Tuesday. Thursday it trades back through the pivot.
questions.simple: Yes, if it triggers again you buy as a brand new trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is trading the loss. After a stop-out you want to go bigger or give the next try more room. A new trade follows every rule again. It gets its own stop and its own size from that stop. It also counts toward 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

questions.q: Bought at 143.20, stop 141.89. You sell a third at 147.13. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. LII broke out on light volume and still ran; the stop was tested to the cent first.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: Our flat base stop is IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit, not the breakout day's low.
questions.why: False. IBD's 7%-8% sell rule is one general guideline. Ours is a few cents under the breakout day's low, which usually sits within about 3% of the buy. The chart sets the stop first, and the size comes from the stop. It is not one fixed percent on every stock.
questions.lesson_line: Our loss is the day's range, not a percent of the price.
questions.simple: False, because our stop sits just under the breakout day's low and not at a fixed percent.

deeper.trap: The trap is mixing two jobs. IBD's 7% to 8% is a limit on how far a purchase may fall. Our stop is placed first from the chart, and the size follows from it. A stop at 7% when the day's low sits much closer is far wider than ours, and it would shrink the size.

questions.q: What stance does the Red reading call for?
choices: Stay mostly in cash and shorts
Full risk, up to 10 positions
Smaller size and fewer positions
Only A+ setups, nothing else
questions.answer: Stay mostly in cash and shorts
questions.why: Mostly cash and shorts. That is the Red stance on our ladder. Green is full risk and up to 10 positions, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Orange is only A+ setups. The textbook base is still worth watching, so you are ready when the reading turns.
questions.lesson_line: The best box in a Red market is a box. Sit on your hands.

wrong.Full risk, up to 10 positions: That is Green. Red sits at the other end of the ladder.
wrong.Smaller size and fewer positions: That is Yellow. Red is further down the ladder than that.
wrong.Only A+ setups, nothing else: That is Orange. Red is further down the ladder than that.

questions.story: The reading is Red. A leader shows a textbook flat base and trades through the pivot on heavy volume.
questions.simple: Red means mostly cash and shorts, however good the chart looks.

deeper.trap: The trap is the chart pull. A textbook base on heavy volume feels like permission. The reading comes first. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, Orange is only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash and shorts.

reasons: asks the ladder stance only; whether Red allows any long is an open owner question

questions.q: How many do you take on day one?
choices: A few; add more as they work
Half now; the rest tomorrow
All eight, each at half size
None; wait a week to be sure
questions.answer: A few; add more as they work
questions.why: A few. After a correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions. Add more only as the first ones work. Green is the ceiling: full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. It is not the first day's order. Many leaders basing sideways after a pullback is the best setting for this setup.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few positions first. Let the winners earn the next ones.

wrong.None; wait a week to be sure: The rule is to start with a few, not to wait. Start small and add as they work.
wrong.Half now; the rest tomorrow: That adds on the clock. The rule adds more only as the first ones work.
wrong.All eight, each at half size: Eight positions is not a few. Start with a few and add as they work.

questions.story: After a correction the reading just turned Green. Your list shows eight flat bases sitting at their pivots.
questions.simple: Start with a few, and add more only as the first ones work.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading Green as go all in. Green says what you may hold: up to 10 positions at full risk per grade. The few-first rule says how you get there. After a correction you earn size one working position at a time.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market; stop under low; third at 3R
Market; base-low stop; all out at 2R
Limit under pivot; 7% stop; third at 3R
Market; stop under low; all out at 5R
questions.answer: Market; stop under low; third at 3R
questions.why: Market, stop under the day's low, and a third at 3R. We buy with a market order as price trades through the pivot, in regular hours. The stop is a few cents under the day's low. The first third comes off at 3R, another at 5R, and the last third trails. NUS reached 3R the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Know the plan before the trigger; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Market; base-low stop; all out at 2R: The base low is not the stop, and the first trim is a third at 3R, not all of it at 2R.
wrong.Limit under pivot; 7% stop; third at 3R: A limit under the pivot may never fill on a breakout. The stop sits under the day's low, not at a fixed percent.
wrong.Market; stop under low; all out at 5R: The last third trails. The first third comes off at 3R and another at 5R, not all at once.

questions.story: NUS, September 2013: six weeks flat, three taps of 90, above a rising 50 and 200-day. It trades through 90 on 1.9x volume.
questions.simple: Buy at market through the pivot, put the stop under the day's low, and sell a third at 3R.

deeper.example: NUS, 2013-09-09: it traded through 90 on 1.9x volume. Buy 90.01, stop 88.22, which is 2.0% under the fill. It reached 3R on day 1, and the scan ran on to 23.5R. A plan made before the trigger lets you act without a debate.

reasons: owner rulebook E57, F62 and B19
fixed before (85.00 was not NUS's base low)

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; only a 5R winner holds
Yes; the trend is still up
No; unless you trim it by half
Yes; the stop covers the gap
questions.why: No. We hold through an earnings report only if the trade is up 5R. At 2R the cushion is too small for a gap you cannot stop. There are also no new buys in the 3 days before a report. Trimming half does not change this: the test is the 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket; 2R does not.

wrong.Yes; the trend is still up: The trend does not report earnings. The gap does.
wrong.No; unless you trim it by half: Trimming does not change the rule: what you still hold must be up 5R.
wrong.Yes; the stop covers the gap: A gap can open through the stop, so the stop is no cover for a report. The 5R cushion is.

questions.story: Your flat base long is up 2R and earnings are tomorrow after the close.
questions.simple: No, because we hold through earnings only when the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2R.

deeper.trap: The trap is the trend. The base is working, so you want to stay. But earnings is a gap you cannot stop, and a gap can open through the stop. At 5R the cushion pays for it. At 2R it does not, whatever the chart looks like.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (B22)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Do its lines pass our card?
choices: Yes; price, 50-day, 200-day stacked
No; the 50-day is under the 200-day
No; price is under the 200-day
Yes; price over the 200-day is enough
questions.why: Yes. On the day before the breakout, price sat above the 50-day and the 200-day, and the 50 sat above the 200. That is the context our card wants. It was a six-week shelf riding the rising 10- and 21-day after the stock nearly doubled. It broke out the next day on 1.9x volume. No longs below the 200-day is the rulebook's hard line.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines before the box. Stacked, rising, price on top: that is context.

wrong.No; the 50-day is under the 200-day: Look again: the 50-day runs above the 200-day here.
wrong.No; price is under the 200-day: Price sits above the 200-day here, riding its shorter averages.
wrong.Yes; price over the 200-day is enough: That is one line. Our card also wants price over the 50-day and the 50-day over the 200-day.

questions.simple: Yes, because price is above both averages and the 50-day is above the 200-day.

deeper.trap: The trap is checking only the 200-day. The rulebook's hard line is no longs below the 200-day. Our card also wants the 50 above the 200, so the order is price, then the 50-day, then the 200-day. That second half is our card's rule, not the rulebook's hard line.

reasons: owner rulebook B26 covers the 200-day only; the 50-over-200 half is our card's rule

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through a flat top. Do its price, 50-day and 200-day pass our card?
choices: No; the 50 is under the 200-day
No; price is under the 200-day
Yes; price is above the 200-day
Yes; recoveries make strong bases
questions.why: No. The 50-day sat under the 200-day, so the order of the lines fails. On the trigger day the close was 14.3% above the 200-day and the 50-day 1.6% under it. This base was built in a recovery out of a downtrend, not by a leader resting. It worked, with a best of 6.3R, and it is still not ours.
questions.lesson_line: A base that works is not always our base. The lines decide before the box does.

wrong.No; price is under the 200-day: Price sat above the 200-day. The line that fails is the 50-day.
wrong.Yes; price is above the 200-day: Price above the 200 is one line of the check. The 50 under the 200 fails the other.
wrong.Yes; recoveries make strong bases: We want a leader resting above a settled 50 over 200 order, not a rebound out of a downtrend. This one did work, but that is not the test.

questions.simple: No, because the 50-day is still under the 200-day, so this is a rebound and not a leader resting.

deeper.counter: The pass costs a winner here: this base reached a best of 6.3R. A rule is judged over many trades, not one. The lines are the order we trade, so we pass even when the pass turns out wrong this once.

reasons: the 50-over-200 half is our card's row (c05), not the owner rulebook's B26

questions.q: IBD counts a breakout as a new stage only when it gained at least 20% before the next base.
questions.why: True. IBD says a breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% to be counted as one stage. A smaller gain does not start a new stage. MarketSmith also resets the base count to 1 once an intraday low undercuts the low of the previous base. Our card counts the same way: first or second base since the last stage reset.
questions.lesson_line: Count stages by the gains between bases, and start over after an undercut.
questions.simple: True, because a breakout counts as a new stage only after it gains at least 20%.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting every pullback or every breakout as a new stage. A breakout that gained less than 20% does not count. The count goes back to 1 only when price undercuts the prior base's low.

reasons: card base-count line is proposed and the owner may change it

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00. The base's first week tops out at 97.50. How far under the high is that, in percent?
questions.why: 2.5%. The gap is the left-side high minus the first week's high, divided by the left-side high. Here that is 100.00 minus 97.50, over 100.00, which is 2.5%. Our card wants the first week within 3% of the left-side high, so this passes. Measure from the high, not from 97.50.
questions.lesson_line: The first week stays close to the high. Measure the gap in percent.
questions.simple: The first week sits 2.5% under the high, and our card allows up to 3%, so it passes.

reasons: the 3% is a proposed card number

questions.q: Does this base pass our card's first-week test?
questions.story: The left-side high is 100.00. The base's first week, the five sessions after that high, tops out at 93.00, which is 7% under it. Then it builds a neat box between 91 and 93.
choices: No; week one fell too far below it
Yes, the box is neat and orderly
Yes, if volume dries up in the box
No; a flat base needs a handle
questions.answer: No; week one fell too far below it
questions.why: No. Our card wants the base's first week to reach within 3% of the left-side high. Here the first week's highest high is 93.00, which is 7% under the top, so it fails. A neat box later does not fix week one. A flat base rests near its high from the start.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base stays near its high in week one. A quick drop fails the test, however neat the box.

wrong.Yes, the box is neat and orderly: A neat box later does not fix week one. The first week must stay near the high.
wrong.Yes, if volume dries up in the box: Quiet volume is a grade cue. It cannot make up for a first week that fell away.
wrong.No; a flat base needs a handle: Handles belong to the cup. A flat base is a box and needs none.

questions.simple: No, because the first week must stay within 3% of the high, and this one fell 7%.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging the box and forgetting where it sits. The box between 91 and 93 can be perfectly tight. But week one fell 7% under the top, so the stock has not rested near its high. It has fallen away and is building a lower shelf.

reasons: the 3% first-week line is a proposed card number

questions.q: Our card caps a flat base at 325 sessions. A trading week has 5 sessions. How many weeks is that?
questions.why: 65 weeks. 325 sessions divided by 5 sessions a week is 65 weeks. Our card allows at most 65 weeks from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. MarketSmith also puts a flat base at 5 to 65 weeks long.
questions.lesson_line: There is a ceiling on length too: 65 weeks, which is 325 sessions.
questions.simple: 325 sessions at 5 sessions a week is 65 weeks, the longest a flat base can run on our card.

questions.q: Is it a flat base breakout?
questions.story: A leader's box began at a left-side high 80 weeks ago. Price has stayed under that high since, tapping it again and again. Today it trades through it.
choices: No; it ran too long to be flat
Yes, a longer base is stronger
Yes, as long as the top is flat
No; it needs a handle first
questions.answer: No; it ran too long to be flat
questions.why: No. Our card caps a flat base at 65 weeks from the left-side high to the day before the breakout. This one went sideways for 80 weeks, so it is too long. MarketSmith puts a flat base at 5 to 65 weeks. A flat top is needed but is not enough. Past the cap it is no longer a flat base.
questions.lesson_line: A base that drags on past 65 weeks is no longer a flat base.

wrong.Yes, a longer base is stronger: Length has a cap. Past 65 weeks it is no longer a flat base.
wrong.Yes, as long as the top is flat: A flat top is needed, but not enough. The base must also be 65 weeks or less.
wrong.No; it needs a handle first: A handle belongs to the cup. The flat base fails here on length.

questions.simple: No, because a flat base can run at most 65 weeks and this one ran 80.

deeper.trap: The trap is a long, tidy base that looks strong. A flat top tapped again and again is good, but the clock matters too. At 80 weeks it is past the cap, so this is not a flat base breakout, whatever the top looks like.

reasons: card cap matches MarketSmith's 5 to 65 weeks

questions.q: Which ceiling is the cleaner one by our card's cue?
questions.story: Two stocks rest under a flat top. Stock A made two clean taps of it, a month apart. Stock B made four, each a separate swing.
choices: Stock B, three or more taps
Stock A, fewer taps mean less supply
Both are identical on our card
Neither; a ceiling needs five taps
questions.answer: Stock B, three or more taps
questions.why: Stock B. Two or more separate touches of the top make a ceiling, so both stocks qualify. Three or more clean taps of one flat level is our card's cleaner version. It is a cue, not a gate, and the final grade stays a judgment call. Stock A still has a ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: Two taps make a ceiling. Three or more make it the cleaner one.

wrong.Stock A, fewer taps mean less supply: More clean taps of one level make the cleaner ceiling on our card, not fewer.
wrong.Both are identical on our card: Both pass as ceilings, but three or more taps is the cleaner version.
wrong.Neither; a ceiling needs five taps: Two or more separate touches make a ceiling. Five is not a rule.

questions.simple: Stock B, because three or more clean taps is the cleaner ceiling, and two taps still count.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking touches can be any days. Touches must be separate, with the first at least 10 sessions back. Four back-to-back days at the top are one push, not four taps.

reasons: card criterion is proposed; our scan found no difference for three or more taps

questions.q: Our card wants the 200-day to be no lower than it was 20 sessions ago.
questions.why: True. On our card the 200-day must be no lower than it was 20 sessions ago. A flat 200-day passes, and a falling one fails. This check sits beside the line order: price above the 50-day and the 200-day, with the 50 above the 200.
questions.lesson_line: Check the slope of the 200-day. It must not be falling.
questions.simple: True, because we do not want the 200-day falling over the last 20 sessions.

reasons: key rests on one card fact

questions.q: Does the context pass our card?
questions.story: A leader rests in a box above its 50-day and 200-day, with the 50-day over the 200-day. The 200-day is 41.80 today and was 42.30 twenty sessions ago.
choices: No; the 200-day is lower now
Yes, price is above both averages
Yes, the 50-day is over the 200-day
No; it needs a rising 10-day
questions.why: No. The 200-day is 41.80 today and was 42.30 twenty sessions ago, so it is lower. Our card wants it no lower than 20 sessions ago. Stacked averages do not make up for that. Price above both averages and the 50 over the 200 are two other checks, and all three must pass. A flat 200-day would pass.
questions.lesson_line: Stacked averages are not enough. The 200-day must not be falling.

wrong.Yes, price is above both averages: That is one check. The 200-day must also not be lower than 20 sessions ago.
wrong.Yes, the 50-day is over the 200-day: That is one check. A falling 200-day still fails the context.
wrong.No; it needs a rising 10-day: The card asks about the 200-day slope, not the 10-day.

questions.simple: No, because the 200-day is now lower than it was 20 sessions ago, even though the averages stack.

deeper.trap: The trap is a small fall. The drop looks tiny, and the averages still stack. But the test is simply no lower than 20 sessions ago, and 41.80 is lower than 42.30.

questions.q: The stock goes vertical. What fits our rule?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 90.01. Two weeks on, it has jumped on gaps three days running, each bar bigger than the last, far over its rising 10-day.
choices: Sell a big part into the surge
Buy more to ride the move
Sit tight until the 21-day breaks
Sell a token slice, hold the rest
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the surge
questions.why: Sell a big part. Into a climax run on your own long, we sell a big part into it. How big a part is a judgment call. Here the stock jumped on gaps three days running, each bar bigger, far over its rising 10-day.
questions.lesson_line: When a winner goes parabolic, sell a big part into it.

wrong.Buy more to ride the move: A burst is a time to sell into strength, not to add.
wrong.Sit tight until the 21-day breaks: The rule is to sell a big part into the burst, not to sit through it.
wrong.Sell a token slice, hold the rest: A token slice is not a big part. The rule sells a big part into the burst.

questions.simple: Sell a big part of the position into the surge, as a judgment call.

deeper.trap: The trap is buying the excitement. Three gap days, each bigger, feel like proof. The rule says the opposite: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long. Bracco's parabolic burst is the model. How big a part is a judgment call.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (C34)
judgment call in the owner rulebook

questions.q: A climax run on a winner is the moment to add to the position.
questions.why: False. Into a climax run on your own long, sell a big part, not add. A climax run is a vertical burst, and it is a moment to take profit. How big a part is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Climax run: sell into strength. Do not add.
questions.simple: False, because a climax run is a time to sell a big part, not to add.

reasons: key rests on one rulebook fact (C34)
judgment call in the owner rulebook

questions.q: Our buy point is the pivot, 48.50. By our no-chase rule, what is the highest price we will pay?
questions.why: 50.44. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. With market orders our buy point is the pivot, because IBD's 10 cents does not matter. Add four percent of the pivot to the pivot. Any price above that is a chase.
questions.lesson_line: Know your top price before the open. Past four percent, I let it go.
questions.simple: Add 4% of the pivot to the pivot, which is 50.44, and never pay more than that.

questions.q: What does the third tap of the top do on our card?
questions.story: A stock rests seven weeks under 52. It has tapped 52 on three separate swings, each within a few cents. The first tap came five weeks back.
choices: Makes the ceiling the A+ version
Makes it a ceiling; two taps do not
Means the top will break this time
Nothing; taps never change the grade
questions.answer: Makes the ceiling the A+ version
questions.why: It makes the A+ version. On our card, three or more clean taps of one flat level is the A+ version of the ceiling. Two or more separate touches already make the ceiling, so the third tap counts toward the grade, not the pass. It is a cue, not a forecast. Our scan found no difference in outcomes with three or more taps.
questions.lesson_line: Two taps make the ceiling. Three or more clean taps make it the A+ version.

wrong.Makes it a ceiling; two taps do not: Two or more separate touches already make the ceiling. The third tap only makes it the A+ version.
wrong.Means the top will break this time: Our card keeps taps as a grade cue. Our scan found no difference in outcomes with three or more taps.
wrong.Nothing; taps never change the grade: Our card lists three or more clean taps as the A+ version of the ceiling, so it counts in the grade.

questions.simple: The third clean tap makes the ceiling the A+ version on our card, but two taps already count.

reasons: card criterion is proposed; our scan found no difference for three or more taps
an earlier three-taps item (q73) was cut in pilot-1

conflicts: Pending-owner criteria kept OUT of every key (the course's current default, waiting on the owner): fb.prior_trend 30% over 65 sessions (D-029; q25 computes a percent only and quotes IBD's 30% as IBD's); fb.length_min 25 sessions / 5 weeks (D-042; no key recalls it, q50 keys the high tight flag on its doubling pole, IBD's five weeks appears only in quotes); fb.depth 15% (D-043; q26 computes depth only; q49 and q51 use 24% and 18.5%, deeper than every option on the card, 15, 12 and 10); fb.breakout_volume 1.4x the 50-day (D-006; never a gate here, a grade cue in q42 and q57, the number never keyed); fb.stop_width what to do when the honest stop is wider than about 3% or the ADR (D-005; q39 keys only 'never pull the stop in', A3/A4, and q54 the XOM lesson); fb.earnings_gap_trigger (D-025; no item); fb.other_entries, the early pivot, the U&R inside the base and the retest (D-027; no item, IBD's early buy point is not keyed).

Base count: the card's gate says first or second base (fb.base_count, proposed) while its B- row says 'third or later'; IBD S1 says flat bases 'tend to form as a second or third base' and S6 'usually not a first-stage structure'. q40 keys a FOURTH base as a pass (IBD S7: late-stage bases often blow up; MarketSmith: third, fourth or later more likely to fail) and never asks about a third base. The owner may want the third base as B- rather than a pass.

Where the base starts: IBD counts from the first down week on a weekly chart (S1, S3); MarketSmith and our card count from the left-side high (S12). q09 keys the left-side high and keeps 'the first down week' out of the choices so IBD's way is never marked wrong.

Anticipating: Bonde anticipates a flat base with a buy stop (S14); Kullamagi finds anticipating less effective (S18); the card lists anticipating with no trigger as a mistake. q05 and q33 key the trade-through; Bonde's view is not quoted.

Volume: IBD requires 40% to 50% above average (S1, S6) and TraderLion 1.4x (S17); Kullamagi is silent; Bulkowski's volume study found heavy-volume breakouts failed more; the owner is 'not a big volume guy'; our scan sided with IBD (39.2% / 30.1% to 3R / 5R against 26.0% / 17.3%). Shallow is better: the card's A+ depth of 10% or less (fb.depth_shallow, D-044) is unmeasured and our scan found 10% or less was NOT better; Bulkowski: 'Tall patterns perform better than short ones.' Not taught here.

Three or more taps as the A+ ceiling (fb.ceiling_three_taps): the scan found no difference. q11 says 'three clean taps is the better version' as the card's cue. Until the 2026-11-10 coverage pass it was never a key; q73 now keys it only as the card's A+ cue, a grade cue and not a gate, and does not cite the scan.
